p.src: Now the man who offered this strategy was Chen Qun, styled Changwen, the Attendant Censor of Documents. Cao Cao asked, “What sound plan have you, Chen Changwen?” Chen Qun said, “Liu Bei and Sun Quan are now as close as lips and teeth. If Liu Bei seeks to take the Western Riverlands, Your Excellency should order a senior general to lead troops, join the forces at Hefei, and march directly upon the Southland; Sun Quan will then surely appeal to Liu Bei for aid. But Liu Bei’s heart is set on the Western Riverlands, so he will surely have no mind to rescue Sun Quan. With no relief, Sun Quan’s strength will fail and his armies weaken; then the lands east of the Yangtze must fall to Your Excellency. Once the lands east of the Yangtze are gained, Jingzhou can be pacified at a single stroke. After Jingzhou is pacified, you may proceed at leisure against the Western Riverlands, and the realm will be settled.” Cao Cao said, “Changwen’s words accord perfectly with my own intent.” He immediately raised a great army of three hundred thousand and marched straight down toward the Southland. He ordered Zhang Liao at Hefei to prepare provisions and fodder for their supply.

p.src: Sun Quan was soon informed by his spies. He assembled his generals to deliberate. Zhang Zhao said, “Send someone to Lu Zijing and have him dispatch an urgent letter to Jingzhou, asking Xuande to join forces with us against Cao Cao. Zijing has shown Xuande kindness, so Xuande will surely heed his words. Moreover, since Xuande is a son-in-law of Eastern Wu, honor will not permit him to refuse. If Xuande comes to our aid, the Southland will have nothing to fear.” Sun Quan followed his counsel and immediately sent a messenger to instruct Lu Su to seek aid from Xuande. Lu Su received the order, wrote a letter at once, and sent a man to deliver it to Xuande. After Xuande read the letter, he lodged the messenger in the guesthouse and sent someone to Nanjun to invite Kongming. When Kongming reached Jingzhou, Xuande gave him Lu Su’s letter to read. Kongming said, “There is no need to mobilize either the troops of the Southland or those of Jingzhou; I shall make Cao Cao afraid even to cast a direct glance toward the southeast.” He then replied to Lu Su, telling him to rest easy without concern. Should the northern army invade, the Imperial Uncle had his own plan to repel it. The messenger departed. Xuande asked, “Cao Cao has now raised an army of three hundred thousand and is coming upon us in one great surge after joining the forces at Hefei. What ingenious plan have you to repel him, Master?” Kongming said, “Throughout his life, Cao Cao has feared above all the troops of Xiliang. Now Cao Cao has killed Ma Teng, whose son Ma Chao presently commands the forces of Xiliang and must bitterly hate the villain Cao Cao. My lord should write to form an alliance with Ma Chao and induce him to raise troops and enter the passes. Cao Cao will then have no leisure to march upon the Southland.” Xuande was delighted. He wrote a letter at once and sent a trusted man straight to Xiliang to deliver it.

p.src: Now Ma Chao, in Xiliang, had a dream one night: he dreamed that he lay upon snowy ground while a pack of tigers came to bite him. He awoke in terror and, troubled at heart, gathered the officers under his command and related the dream. One man beneath his tent immediately said, “This dream is an ill omen.” They looked and saw his trusted commandant Pang De, styled Lingming. Ma Chao asked, “What is your interpretation, Lingming?” Pang De said, “To encounter tigers on snowy ground is a most ominous portent. Can some misfortune have befallen the old general in Xuchang?” Before he had finished, a man stumbled in, fell weeping to the ground, and cried, “My uncle and my younger brothers are all dead!” Ma Chao looked and saw that it was Ma Dai. Ma Chao questioned him in alarm. Ma Dai said, “My uncle conspired with Attendant Gentleman Huang Kui to kill Cao Cao, but unhappily the plot was exposed, and both were beheaded in the marketplace. My two younger brothers were also slain. I alone disguised myself as a merchant and escaped by traveling through the night.”

p.src: On hearing this, Ma Chao wept and collapsed to the ground. His generals helped him up. Ma Chao ground his teeth in bitter hatred of the villain Cao Cao. Suddenly it was reported that the Imperial Uncle Liu of Jingzhou had sent a man bearing a letter. Ma Chao opened and read it. In substance, it said: “I humbly reflect that misfortune has befallen the house of Han. The villain Cao Cao monopolizes power, deceives the sovereign and defies his superiors, while the common people languish. In former days, I received the secret edict together with your late honored father, and we swore to destroy this traitor. Now that your late honored father has been murdered by Cao Cao, he is your enemy with whom you cannot share heaven and earth or behold the same sun and moon. If you can lead the troops of Xiliang to attack Cao Cao’s right flank, I shall raise the forces of Jingzhou and Xiangyang to check his front. Then the rebel Cao Cao may be captured, his treacherous faction destroyed, your vengeance and disgrace redressed, and the house of Han restored. A letter cannot convey all I would say; I await your reply with the utmost urgency.”

p.src: When Ma Chao finished reading, he wiped away his tears and wrote an immediate reply. He sent the messenger back ahead of him, then began mustering the troops of Xiliang. Just as he was about to advance, Han Sui, the Governor of Xiliang, sent someone to invite Ma Chao to a meeting. When Ma Chao reached Han Sui’s residence, Han Sui produced a letter from Cao Cao and showed it to him. It read: “If you seize Ma Chao and convey him to the capital at Xu, I shall at once enfeoff you as Marquis of Xiliang.” Ma Chao prostrated himself and said, “Uncle, please bind the two of us brothers and send us under guard to Xuchang, sparing yourself the labor of taking up arms.” Han Sui helped him up and said, “Your father and I swore brotherhood. How could I bear to harm you? If you raise an army, I shall assist you.”

p.src: Ma Chao bowed in gratitude. Han Sui then had Cao Cao’s messenger dragged out and beheaded, mustered the troops of the eight divisions under his command, and set forth together with Ma Chao. Who commanded these eight divisions? They were Hou Xuan, Cheng Yin, Li Kan, Zhang Heng, Liang Xing, Cheng Yi, Ma Wan, and Yang Qiu. The eight generals followed Han Sui and joined Pang De and Ma Dai under Ma Chao, raising a great army of two hundred thousand that swept toward Chang’an. Zhong Yao, Governor of Chang’an, sent an urgent report to Cao Cao. Meanwhile, he led his army out to meet the enemy and drew up his battle lines in the open country. Ma Dai, vanguard of the Xiliang forces, led fifteen thousand troops onward in a mighty flood that covered hills and fields. Zhong Yao rode out to parley. Ma Dai wielded a treasured saber and engaged Zhong Yao in combat. Before a single bout was finished, Zhong Yao was routed and fled, with Ma Dai pursuing, saber in hand. Ma Chao and Han Sui arrived with the main army and surrounded Chang’an, while Zhong Yao mounted the walls and held them in defense.

p.src: Chang’an had been the capital of the Western Han. Its walls and outer defenses were strong, and its moat was deep and perilous, so it could not be taken by a sudden assault. They laid siege for ten days in succession but could not breach it. Pang De offered a plan: “The soil within Chang’an is hard, and its water is bitter and brackish, scarcely fit to drink. Moreover, there is no firewood. After ten days under siege, soldiers and people alike are suffering hunger. We would do better to withdraw for the moment. We need only do thus and so, and Chang’an will fall into our hands with ease.” Ma Chao said, “An excellent plan!” He immediately sent command flags bearing the character “order” among all the divisions, directing every unit to withdraw. Ma Chao personally guarded the rear while the several armies gradually retired.

p.src: Now Zhong Yao’s younger brother, Zhong Jin, was guarding the western gate. Near the third watch, a fire suddenly broke out inside the gate. As Zhong Jin hurried to extinguish it, a rider swept around beside the wall, raised his saber, and shouted, “Pang De is here!” Caught unprepared, Zhong Jin was cut from his horse with one stroke by Pang De. Pang De scattered the troops, smashed the barrier, severed the locks, and admitted the forces of Ma Chao and Han Sui into the city. Zhong Yao abandoned the city and fled through the eastern gate. Ma Chao and Han Sui took the city and rewarded the whole army for its labors.

p.src: Zhong Yao withdrew to defend Tong Pass and sent an urgent report to Cao Cao. When Cao Cao learned that Chang’an was lost, he dared speak no more of a southern expedition. He summoned Cao Hong and Xu Huang and instructed them: “Take ten thousand troops ahead of me and relieve Zhong Yao in the strict defense of Tong Pass. If the pass is lost within ten days, you shall both be beheaded. If it is lost after ten days, neither of you shall be held responsible. I shall follow shortly with the main army.” The two received their orders and set out at once, traveling through the night. Cao Ren remonstrated, “Cao Hong is impetuous by nature. I truly fear he may mishandle the affair.” Cao Cao said, “You shall escort the provisions and fodder for me, then follow after them to give support.”

p.src: Now Cao Hong and Xu Huang arrived at Tong Pass and took over its firm defense from Zhong Yao, refusing all battle. Ma Chao led his army beneath the pass and heaped abuse upon three generations of Cao Cao's family. Cao Hong flew into a rage and meant to lead his troops down from the pass to fight. Xu Huang remonstrated, “Ma Chao is trying to provoke you into fighting; you must not engage him. When the Prime Minister's main army arrives, he will surely have a plan.” Day and night Ma Chao's troops took turns hurling insults. Cao Hong was bent on fighting, but Xu Huang repeatedly held him back. On the ninth day, looking down from the pass, they saw that the Xiliang troops had all dismounted and were sitting on the grass before the gates; most appeared exhausted and lay sleeping on the ground. Cao Hong at once ordered the horses saddled, mustered three thousand soldiers, and charged down from the pass. The Xiliang soldiers abandoned their horses, cast away their spears, and fled, while Cao Hong pursued them ever farther.

p.src: At the time, Xu Huang was inspecting the provisions atop the pass. Hearing that Cao Hong had gone down to fight, he was greatly alarmed and hastened after him with troops, loudly calling for Cao Hong to turn back; suddenly, a tremendous battle cry rose behind them as Ma Dai led his troops into the attack. As Cao Hong and Xu Huang hurried back, a drum thundered, and two armies swept out from behind the hills: Ma Chao on the left and Pang De on the right. A fierce melee followed. Cao Hong could not withstand them. After losing more than half his troops, he broke through the encirclement and fled back to the pass. The Xiliang troops pursued close behind, and Cao Hong and the others abandoned the pass and fled. Pang De pursued them beyond Tong Pass, but ran into Cao Ren's troops, who rescued Cao Hong and his men. Ma Chao came to support Pang De, and together they took possession of the pass.

p.src: Having lost Tong Pass, Cao Hong fled back to Cao Cao. Cao Cao said, “I gave you a limit of ten days. How did you lose Tong Pass after only nine?” Cao Hong replied, “The Xiliang troops insulted us in every possible way. Seeing their army off guard, I seized the opportunity to pursue them, never imagining I would fall into the rebels' treacherous scheme.” Cao Cao said, “Cao Hong is young, rash, and violent, but you, Xu Huang, should have known better!” Xu Huang said, “I remonstrated with him repeatedly, but he would not listen. That day I was inspecting provisions atop the pass; by the time I learned what had happened, the young general had already gone down from the pass. Fearing disaster, I hurried after him, but he had already fallen into the rebels' treacherous scheme.”

p.src: Cao Cao flew into a rage and ordered Cao Hong beheaded. The officers pleaded for mercy, and Cao Hong acknowledged his guilt and withdrew. Cao Cao advanced his army straight to Tong Pass. Cao Ren said, “We should first establish a fortified camp; it will not be too late to attack the pass afterward.” Cao Cao ordered trees felled and palisades raised, dividing the army into three camps: Cao Ren held the left, Xiahou Yuan the right, and Cao Cao himself occupied the center. The next day, Cao Cao led the officers of all ranks from the three camps in an assault toward the pass and met the Xiliang army head-on. Both sides drew up their battle lines. Cao Cao rode out beneath the commander's banner and saw that every Xiliang soldier was bold and vigorous, every man a hero. He also saw Ma Chao, whose face was as fair as if powdered and whose lips were red as vermilion; he had a slender waist and broad shoulders, a mighty voice and tremendous strength; clad in a white robe and silver armor, long spear in hand, he sat his horse before the formation; Pang De stood above him and Ma Dai below. Cao Cao secretly marveled. Riding forward, he addressed Ma Chao: “You are descended from a renowned general of the Han. Why have you rebelled?” Ma Chao ground his teeth and cursed, “Cao Cao, you traitor! You deceive the sovereign and defy your superiors; even death cannot expiate your crimes! You murdered my father and brothers—our enmity cannot exist beneath the same heaven! I shall take you alive and devour your flesh!”

p.src: With that, he leveled his spear and charged straight at Cao Cao. Yu Jin rode out from behind Cao Cao to meet him. The two riders fought for eight or nine bouts, and Yu Jin fled in defeat. Zhang He rode out against him, but after twenty bouts he too was defeated and fled. Li Tong then came forward. Ma Chao fought with redoubled fury and within a few bouts thrust Li Tong beneath his horse with a single spear stroke. Ma Chao swept his spear backward in signal, and the Xiliang troops charged forward as one. Cao Cao's army suffered a crushing defeat. The Xiliang troops attacked with irresistible force, and none of the officers on either flank could withstand them. Ma Chao, Pang De, and Ma Dai led more than a hundred riders straight into the center to seize Cao Cao. Amid the chaos, Cao Cao heard the Xiliang troops shouting, “The man in the red robe is Cao Cao!” Cao Cao hastily stripped off his red robe while still on horseback, only to hear them shout, “The man with the long beard is Cao Cao!” In terror, Cao Cao drew the sword at his waist and cut off his beard. Someone in the army informed Ma Chao that Cao Cao had cut off his beard. Ma Chao then ordered his men to shout, “Seize the man with the short beard—that is Cao Cao!” When Cao Cao heard this, he tore off a corner of a banner, wrapped it around his neck, and fled. Ma Chao then ordered his men to shout, “Seize the man with the short beard—that is Cao Cao!”
When Cao Cao heard this, he tore off a corner of a banner, wrapped it around his neck, and fled.
A later poet wrote:

p.src: As Cao Cao fled, a lone rider came pursuing from behind. He looked back and saw that it was Ma Chao. Cao Cao was greatly alarmed. Seeing Ma Chao approach, the officers around Cao Cao each fled for his life, abandoning Cao Cao alone. Ma Chao thundered, “Cao Cao, do not flee!” Cao Cao was so terrified that he dropped his horsewhip. Just as he was about to catch him, Ma Chao thrust his spear at Cao Cao from behind. Cao Cao fled around a tree. Ma Chao's spear struck the tree, and by the time he had wrenched it free, Cao Cao was already far away. Ma Chao spurred after him, but a general emerged beside a hillside and cried, “Do not harm my lord! Cao Hong is here!” Brandishing his sword, he spurred forward and barred Ma Chao's way. Cao Cao escaped with his life. Cao Hong fought Ma Chao for forty or fifty bouts, but gradually his swordsmanship grew disordered and his strength began to fail. Xiahou Yuan arrived with several dozen riders. Ma Chao, being alone, feared they might ensnare him, so he wheeled his horse and withdrew; Xiahou Yuan did not pursue.

p.src: Cao Cao returned to camp and found that Cao Ren had defended the palisades to the death; thus the army had suffered no great further losses. Entering his tent, Cao Cao sighed, “Had I put Cao Hong to death, today I would surely have died at Ma Chao's hands!” He then summoned Cao Hong and rewarded him lavishly. He rallied the defeated troops and held the fortified camp fast; the moats were deepened, the ramparts raised, and no one was permitted to go out and fight. Each day Ma Chao led troops before the camp to hurl insults and challenge them to battle, but Cao Cao ordered his soldiers to hold firm, declaring that anyone who moved without orders would be beheaded. The generals said, “All the Xiliang troops wield long spears; we should select archers and crossbowmen to meet them.” Cao Cao replied, “Whether we fight or refrain from fighting rests entirely with me, not with the rebels. Though they possess long spears, how can they strike us at will? My lords need only hold the defenses and watch; the rebels will withdraw of themselves.” The generals privately discussed among themselves, “Whenever the Prime Minister has gone to war before, he has always led from the front; now that Ma Chao has defeated him, why has he become so timid?”

p.src: Several days later, a scout reported, “Ma Chao has received twenty thousand fresh troops from the Qiang tribes to aid him in battle.” Cao Cao was delighted to hear this. His generals asked, “Why is the Chancellor pleased that Ma Chao has gained reinforcements?” Cao Cao replied, “When I have won, I shall explain it to you.” Three days later, another report came that still more troops had arrived at the pass. Again Cao Cao rejoiced and held a celebratory feast in his tent. The generals all laughed to themselves. Cao Cao said, “You gentlemen laugh because you think I have no plan to defeat Ma Chao. What sound strategies have you?” Xu Huang stepped forward and said, “The Chancellor’s main force is gathered here, and the rebels likewise appear to have massed their entire army at the pass. West of the river they must be unprepared. If a force secretly crosses at Puban Ford and first cuts off the rebels’ retreat, while the Chancellor advances directly north of the river to attack them, they will be unable to support either front and must fall into peril.” Cao Cao said, “Gongming’s words accord exactly with my own intentions.” He ordered Xu Huang to lead four thousand picked troops with Zhu Ling in a direct strike west of the river and lie concealed in a mountain valley: “When I cross north of the river, attack at the same time.” Xu Huang and Zhu Ling accepted the order and secretly departed first with the four thousand troops. Cao Cao then ordered Cao Hong to prepare boats and rafts at Puban Ford. Leaving Cao Ren to guard the camp, Cao Cao personally led his troops across the Wei River. A scout soon carried the news to Ma Chao. Ma Chao said, “Cao Cao is not attacking Tong Pass but has men preparing boats and rafts. He means to cross north of the river and surely intends to cut off our rear. I shall lead a force across the river and hold the northern bank against him. If Cao Cao’s troops cannot cross, the provisions east of the river will be exhausted in less than twenty days and his army will surely fall into disorder. Then we can follow the southern bank and strike him, and Cao Cao may be captured.” Han Sui said, “There is no need for that. Have you not heard the maxim of war: ‘Strike when the enemy is halfway across’?” Wait until half of Cao Cao’s army has crossed, then attack from the southern bank, and all his troops will perish in the river.” Ma Chao said, “Uncle’s counsel is excellent.” He immediately sent men to learn when Cao Cao would cross the river.

p.src: Now Cao Cao finished ordering his army, divided it into three bodies, and began crossing the Wei River with the first. By the time the men and horses were upon the river, the sun was just rising. Cao Cao first sent picked troops across to the northern bank to establish a camp. He himself sat on the southern bank with his hand on his sword, accompanied by a hundred personal guards and officers, watching the army cross. Suddenly someone reported, “The white-robed general is coming from the rear!” Everyone recognized Ma Chao and surged aboard the boats. At the riverside, the soldiers clamored without cease as they fought to board. Cao Cao remained seated and unmoved, pointing with the hand upon his sword for them to cease their clamor. Amid shouts and neighing horses, the enemy swarmed toward them. A general leapt from a boat onto the bank and cried, “The rebels are here! Chancellor, please board the boat!” Cao Cao looked and saw that it was Xu Chu. Yet Cao Cao still said, “What matter if the rebels have come?” But when he looked back, Ma Chao was already little more than a hundred paces away. When Xu Chu dragged Cao Cao toward the boat, it had already pulled more than ten feet from shore. Xu Chu hoisted Cao Cao onto his back and leapt aboard. All the accompanying officers and soldiers plunged into the water, clutched the sides of the boat, and struggled to board and save their lives. The small boat was about to capsize. Xu Chu drew his sword and slashed wildly, severing every hand gripping its sides and casting the men into the water; then he hurriedly drove the boat downstream. Xu Chu stood in the stern and hastily poled the boat onward. Cao Cao crouched at Xu Chu’s feet. Ma Chao reached the riverbank and saw the boat already drifting in midstream. He nocked an arrow and ordered his fierce officers to pursue along the bank and shoot; arrows fell as thick and swift as rain. Fearing Cao Cao would be struck, Xu Chu raised a saddle in his left hand to shield him. Ma Chao never loosed an arrow in vain; the boatman fell into the water the instant the bowstring sounded. Dozens of men in the boat were also shot down. With no one able to steady it, the boat spun about in the swift current. Xu Chu alone displayed his divine prowess: gripping the rudder between his legs to work it, he poled the boat with one hand and held up the saddle with the other to protect Cao Cao.

p.src: At that time Ding Fei, magistrate of Weinan County, was on the southern hills. Seeing Ma Chao pressing Cao Cao so fiercely and fearing for Cao Cao’s life, he drove every ox and horse out of his encampment until cattle and horses covered the hills and fields. At the sight, the Xiliang troops all turned back and fought to seize the livestock, abandoning the pursuit; Cao Cao thereby escaped. As soon as he reached the northern bank, he had the boats and rafts scuttled. When the generals heard that Cao Cao was fleeing for his life on the river, they hastened to rescue him, but he had already come ashore. Xu Chu wore heavy armor, and arrows were embedded all over it. The generals escorted Cao Cao to a field camp, where they all knelt and inquired after his safety. Cao Cao laughed loudly and said, “Today I was nearly cornered by that young rebel!” Xu Chu said, “Had someone not released horses and cattle to lure the rebels away, they would surely have crossed the river in force.” Cao Cao asked, “Who lured the rebels away?” Someone who knew replied, “Ding Fei, magistrate of Weinan County.” Shortly afterward, Ding Fei entered to see him. Cao Cao thanked him, saying, “But for your excellent stratagem, I would have been captured by the rebels.” He then appointed Ding Fei Commandant of Army Administration. Ding Fei said, “Though the rebels have withdrawn for the moment, they will surely return tomorrow. We must use a sound strategy to resist them.” Cao Cao said, “I have already made preparations.” He summoned his generals and ordered, “Divide your forces and build covered ways along the river to serve for now as the base of our camp defenses. When the rebels come, array the troops outside the covered ways, while leaving the inside empty with banners standing there as a feint. Also dig trenches along the river and conceal them with loose earth and wooden lattices, then use troops by the river to draw the enemy on. If the rebels rush upon us, they will surely fall in; once they do, we can capture them.”

p.src: Now Ma Chao returned to Han Sui and said, “I nearly captured Cao Cao, but a general fought fiercely, carried him onto a boat, and escaped. I do not know who the man was.” Han Sui said, “I have heard that Cao Cao selected men of extraordinary strength as guards before his tent, calling them the Tiger Guard, and placed the fierce generals Dian Wei and Xu Chu in command. Dian Wei is dead, so the man who saved Cao Cao must have been Xu Chu. His courage and strength surpass those of ordinary men, and everyone calls him the ‘Tiger Fool.’ If you encounter him, do not underestimate him.” Ma Chao said, “I too have long heard his name.” Han Sui said, “Now that Cao Cao has crossed the river, he means to strike our rear. We must attack swiftly and not allow him to establish a camp. Once his camp is established, it will be exceedingly difficult to destroy.” Ma Chao said, “In my humble opinion, the best plan is still to hold the northern bank and prevent him from crossing.” Han Sui said, “Worthy nephew, you guard the camp while I lead troops along the river to fight Cao Cao. What say you?” Ma Chao said, “Have Pang De serve as vanguard and accompany you, Uncle.”

p.src: Thereupon Han Sui and Pang De led fifty thousand troops straight toward Weinan. Cao Cao ordered his generals to lure them between the two sides of the covered ways. Pang De led more than a thousand armored horsemen in the first charge. As battle cries arose, men and horses alike plunged into the concealed pits. Pang De sprang high and leapt out of the pit onto level ground. He killed several men where he stood, then hacked his way on foot through the encirclement. Han Sui had already been trapped at the heart of the encirclement. Pang De went on foot to rescue him and encountered Cao Yong, an officer under Cao Ren. With a single stroke Pang De cut him from his horse, seized the mount, carved a bloody path through the enemy, rescued Han Sui, and fled southeast. Cao Cao’s troops pursued from behind, but Ma Chao led troops to their aid and defeated the pursuers. They also rescued more than half their troops and horses. They fought until sunset before returning. When the men and horses were counted, the officers Cheng Yin and Zhang Heng were found lost, along with more than two hundred men killed in the pits. Ma Chao and Han Sui conferred: “If we delay for long, Cao Cao will establish a camp north of the river, and it will be difficult to drive back the enemy. Better to take light cavalry tonight and raid his field camp.” Han Sui said, “We must divide the force so the front and rear can support one another.” Thereupon Ma Chao took command of the vanguard and ordered Pang De and Ma Dai to provide support from the rear. They set out that very night.

p.src: Now Cao Cao withdrew his troops and encamped north of the Wei River. Summoning his generals, he said, “The rebels know that we have not yet established our stockade, and they are certain to raid our field camp. Scatter troops in ambush on every side, and leave the central camp empty. When the signal cannon sounds, let every ambushing force rise at once; we shall capture them in a single charge.” The generals obeyed his command and completed their dispositions for the ambush. That night, however, Ma Chao first sent Cheng Yi ahead with thirty horsemen to reconnoiter. Seeing neither men nor horses, Cheng Yi rode straight into the central camp. When Cao Cao’s troops saw the Xiliang horsemen arrive, they fired the signal cannon. The ambushing troops sprang out from every side, only to find that they had surrounded a mere thirty riders. Cheng Yi was slain by Xiahou Yuan. But Ma Chao, together with Pang De and Ma Dai, came surging in from the rear, their forces divided into three columns. Indeed:
